topic: Retrofit, OkHttp & Ktor client: networking in practice

questions.question: The server returns 404 for this Retrofit call. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The call throws `retrofit2.HttpException`
Returning `Response<User>` lets you read the status without an exception
It returns null because the response has no User body
`HttpException.code()` returns 404
questions.explanation: For a suspend function returning the body type directly, Retrofit throws `HttpException` for any non-2xx response; its `code()` and `response()` give the details. Declaring `Response<User>` returns normally for every HTTP status, so you can check `isSuccessful` yourself. It never silently returns null for an error.

questions.question: A Retrofit `suspend` function can be called from `Dispatchers.Main`, because Retrofit runs the request on OkHttp's own background threads.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Retrofit's suspend support uses OkHttp's asynchronous `enqueue` and suspends until the callback arrives, so the calling thread is never blocked. Wrapping such calls in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` is unnecessary, although parsing large responses may still be worth moving off Main.

questions.question: Why should an app share one `OkHttpClient` instead of creating one per request or per API?
options: Each client has its own connection pool and threads; sharing reuses them
OkHttpClient isn't thread-safe, so only one instance can exist at a time
Retrofit throws an exception if two clients are created in one process
Separate clients share one cookie jar, which leaks cookies between APIs
questions.explanation: Every client owns a connection pool and dispatcher threads, so sharing one lets requests reuse warm connections and saves memory. If an API needs different settings, derive a client with `client.newBuilder()`, which shares the pool. `OkHttpClient` is thread-safe and designed to be shared.

questions.question: Where is the idiomatic place in OkHttp to refresh an expired access token when the server responds 401?
options: An Authenticator, which OkHttp calls on 401 and which returns a retry request or null
An application interceptor that catches the HttpException thrown by the Retrofit call
A custom Retrofit CallAdapter that retries every failed call once with a new token
A custom Dns implementation that routes failed requests to the auth server instead
questions.explanation: OkHttp calls `Authenticator.authenticate()` when a response is 401; you return the request with a new token to retry it, or null to give up. `HttpException` is created by Retrofit after OkHttp has finished, so an interceptor never sees it. An interceptor can also handle 401s, but then you reimplement retry limits that the Authenticator already gives you.

questions.question: Five requests run in parallel and all get 401 at the same moment. Each triggers a token refresh, and the server invalidates refresh tokens after one use, so the user is logged out. What's the usual fix?
options: Synchronize the refresh, and skip it if the failed request's token is already stale
Use addNetworkInterceptor instead of addInterceptor, so that only one request runs at a time
Call retryOnConnectionFailure(false) so that OkHttp stops sending the 401 requests again
Make the connection pool larger so the five requests no longer share a single connection
questions.explanation: Guard the refresh with a lock, and inside it compare the token on the failed request with the current one; if another thread already refreshed it, just retry with the new token. Only the first caller then performs the refresh. Interceptor type, connection-failure retries and pool size have no effect on how many refreshes run.

questions.question: Which statements about OkHttp interceptors are true? Select all that apply.
options: Application interceptors run once per call, even if OkHttp follows redirects
Network interceptors aren't invoked for responses served from the cache
Network interceptors see headers OkHttp adds, like Accept-Encoding: gzip
Application interceptors can't return their own Response to short-circuit
Network interceptors run before the application interceptors do
questions.explanation: Application interceptors (`addInterceptor`) wrap the whole call, including cache and retries, and may return a response without calling `proceed`. Network interceptors (`addNetworkInterceptor`) sit next to the wire, so they run once per actual network request, see the final headers, and are skipped on a cache hit. Application interceptors run first, on the outside of the chain.

questions.question: What is `ContentNegotiation` with `json()` for in this Ktor client?
options: Serializing bodies and parsing responses with body<User>() via kotlinx.serialization
Choosing between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 for each request, based on the server's support
Retrying failed requests with backoff until a response with a usable body arrives
Compressing request bodies with gzip and decompressing the server's responses
questions.explanation: `ContentNegotiation` maps Kotlin objects to and from the HTTP body using a registered converter, here kotlinx.serialization JSON, and sets `Content-Type`/`Accept` to match. That is what makes `setBody(user)` and `response.body<User>()` work. Retries and compression come from other plugins (`HttpRequestRetry`, `ContentEncoding`), and the HTTP version is up to the engine.

questions.question: With Ktor client 3.x and no other configuration, the server answers 404 with an error JSON body. What happens on this line?
options: No status exception (expectSuccess is false); parsing the error body as User fails
It throws ClientRequestException, because Ktor always throws for any 4xx status by default
It returns null, because Ktor can't deserialize a successful body from a 404 response
It retries the request three times and then throws the last ResponseException it got
questions.explanation: Since Ktor 2, `expectSuccess` defaults to false, so non-2xx responses are returned normally. `body<User>()` then tries to turn the error JSON into a `User`, which fails with a deserialization error that hides the real cause. Check `response.status` first, or set `expectSuccess = true` to get `ClientRequestException`/`ServerResponseException`.

questions.question: OkHttp's `retryOnConnectionFailure` (on by default) makes it retry a request whose server responded with HTTP 500.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That setting is about connection-level failures, such as a stale pooled connection or an unreachable route, not about HTTP responses. A 500 is a valid response, and OkHttp returns it as is. Retrying on server errors is up to you, for example in an interceptor, and only for idempotent requests.

questions.question: The ViewModel is cleared while this runs. What happens to the HTTP request?
options: execute() keeps blocking until the request ends; only Retrofit's suspend API cancels the call
Retrofit cancels the underlying OkHttp call immediately, in exactly the same way as with suspend
The IO thread is interrupted, so execute() throws an InterruptedException straight away
The response is still returned to load()'s caller even though the coroutine was cancelled
questions.explanation: Coroutine cancellation is cooperative and does not stop a blocked thread, so `execute()` runs to completion or timeout; `withContext` then throws `CancellationException` and the result is dropped. A `suspend` Retrofit function is cancellation-aware: cancelling the coroutine calls `Call.cancel()` on the OkHttp call. This is one reason to prefer suspend functions over `Call<T>.execute()`.
